Madhuri, you look like a girl whose friend has stopped talking to her. Come, I'll tell you what I did at fifteen. I'm your Dolma Aunty, and I learned this the hard way.

Soon I didn't even decide it. The moment Vaibhav's voice got an edge, I'd go polite. "Sure." "Okay." "Whatever you think."
We stopped fighting. We also stopped talking about anything real: his job move, my brother's loan, the holiday we'd cancelled. All of it went behind a wall of "fine."
The house was peaceful. Ma kept asking why her son had gone so quiet. And it felt like living with a stranger.

qa.q: What was the first big fight about?
qa.a: It was about money.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when he went quiet the first time?
qa.a: Mohit felt relief, because the shouting stopped and silence seemed to work.

qa.q: What turning point could Mohit have used before silence became automatic?
qa.a: Mohit could have told Vaibhav about needing a break and set a time to come back to the job move and the holiday, instead of letting "fine" end every talk.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav likely experiencing during that year?
qa.a: He probably felt shut out and lonely, living with polite answers while real issues piled up unspoken.

grounding: A young man recalls how silence first ended the shouting, then became his automatic answer, with unresolved issues piling up behind politeness.

Lakshmi spoke most of today. She described how, in the first months of marriage, Lokesh would go quiet after arguments and the shouting would stop. "I was grateful," she said.
Now, she says, he goes polite the moment she raises anything: his late nights, his parents' visits, the savings account they never discussed. "He says, 'Sure, whatever you want,' and nothing changes."
Lokesh sat with his arms crossed. When I asked what happens inside him, he said, "Silence works. It stops the fighting."
I noted that the fighting stopped, but the issues remain. I've asked them each to write down three topics they've avoided, for next week.

Wednesday, late

Lavanya asked again tonight about visiting her parents for Diwali. I said, "Sure, we'll see." Same thing I said last month about the car. Same thing about the rent increase.
When did I become this guy? The first time I went quiet was after our fight about my job, and it felt like a miracle. No shouting. So I kept doing it.
Now I don't even think. Her voice goes up, and I go polite. Maa says I'm "such a calm son." If only she knew.
There's a whole pile of things we haven't talked about, and it's getting taller. I don't know how to start taking it down.
— Hrithik

Devika had tried everything. For three days after the fight, Alok came home from the post office, ate, said "hmm," and went to sleep.
On the first day she asked questions. "What's wrong? Tell me." On the second, she cried in the courtyard where the neighbours could hear. On the third, she cooked his favourite kadhi and waited. He ate it without a word.
In their small house by the canal, the silence was louder than the tractors outside.
On the fourth evening, when he came in, Devika didn't get up. She kept sorting the rice, back straight, face closed. If he could shut her out, she could shut him out too. But inside she felt like a girl of six again, waiting for someone to notice her.

qa.q: What did Devika cook on the third day?
qa.a: His favourite kadhi.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling on the fourth evening?
qa.a: She felt hurt, powerless and angry, and underneath like a small girl again, waiting to be noticed.

qa.q: What turning point is available now?
qa.a: Devika could tell Alok plainly how invisible his silence makes her feel, or ask a trusted elder to help them talk, before both of them go cold.

qa.q: What is Alok likely experiencing?
qa.a: He may be overwhelmed or stuck in silence after the fight, perhaps not realising how deeply it is hurting Devika.

grounding: A young wife tries questions, tears and kindness to reach her silent husband, then goes cold herself as hurt turns to anger.

It had been five days since Thabo last said more than "yes" or "no" to Fatima.
In their flat in Johannesburg, she had tried asking gently, then asking loudly. She had cried in the bathroom, then in front of him. She had left a note on his pillow. He'd folded it and put it in the drawer.
On the sixth day, Fatima stopped. She made her own coffee. She didn't say goodbye when she left for work. When Thabo asked, "What time will you be back?", she said, "Does it matter?"
She felt cold and hard. Underneath, though, was an old ache, the same one from when she was small and nobody at home had time for her.

qa.q: What did Thabo do with Fatima's note?
qa.a: He folded it and put it in the drawer.

qa.q: What was Fatima feeling underneath her coldness on the sixth day?
qa.a: She felt hurt and invisible, with an old ache of not mattering, which had turned into anger and coldness.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this stage?
qa.a: Fatima could tell Thabo about the old ache his silence touches, or they could seek a counsellor's help before both freeze.

qa.q: What might Thabo be experiencing when Fatima says "Does it matter?"
qa.a: He may feel surprised and stung, realising for the first time that his silence has pushed her away.

grounding: A young woman shut out by her partner's silence tries questions, tears and notes, then goes cold herself as old fears of not mattering surface.

passage:
The flat in Chennai had gone very quiet. For two weeks, Madhav and Chandrika hadn't said a word about the fight, the one about whether to move to Dubai for his job.
They talked about other things. "Milk's finished." "Your mother called." "The plumber is coming Thursday."
Each evening Madhav thought: she should bring it up, she's the one who got so angry. Each evening Chandrika thought: he should bring it up, it's his job, his decision.
Both were afraid that bringing it up would bring back the shouting. Both were too proud to go first.
The offer letter lay on the dining table, under the fruit bowl, getting a little more yellow every day.

qa.q: Where was the offer letter lying?
qa.a: On the dining table, under the fruit bowl.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling during those two weeks?
qa.a: He felt proud and afraid, waiting for Chandrika to bring it up because he feared another shouting match.

qa.q: What turning point is available to them at this stage?
qa.a: One of them could name the freeze, for example, "We haven't talked about the letter. I'm scared of another fight, but I want to," breaking the waiting game.

qa.q: What is Chandrika experiencing during the freeze?
qa.a: She is also proud and afraid, waiting for Madhav to go first and quietly feeling the distance grow.

grounding: A young couple both avoid the subject of a big fight, each waiting for the other to move, stuck by pride and fear while distance grows.
